tagline: Hilltop stage stops and connected farm buildings trace a working valley.
intro: The Branch River Valley Trail threads woodlands, open pastures, rivers and streams through Wakefield and Milton toward the Maine border. Visit New Hampshire’s byway guide presents this as a journey through the state’s agricultural, industrial and tourism heritage, with views of the Belknap Range. Its landmarks include the hilltop village of Wakefield Corner and the working demonstration farm at the New Hampshire Farm Museum.

Wakefield developed as a stop for sledges and stagecoaches traveling between the seacoast and the White Mountains. The Portsmouth, Great Falls and Conway Railroad’s arrival in 1871 shifted the town’s center from Wakefield Corner to Sanbornville. Civic life followed: a new town hall opened in Sanbornville in 1895, replacing the older hall in Wakefield village. The earlier village retains its 1836 town hall, library, Grange Hall and one-room schoolhouse. Sanbornville remains Wakefield’s retail district, while the museum in Milton continues to use its open fields for a working demonstration farm.

Begin at Wakefield Corner and follow Route 153 south to Sanbornville at Lovell Lake’s outlet, where the Branch River begins. Continue to Union, then take Route 125 toward the Farm Museum and Milton. Milton’s main village lies beside the Salmon Falls River at the outlet of Milton Pond, with Maine across the river.

moments.title: Wakefield Corner
moments.text: Wakefield Corner’s old town hall marks the village’s former role as the civic center. Built in 1836, it hosted town meetings until the new hall opened in Sanbornville in 1895. The change followed the railway’s arrival, which had shifted the town center away from this hilltop stage stop. The historic district also includes a library, a Grange Hall and a one-room schoolhouse now housing the historical society. After its civic service, the old hall was leased to the Congregational Church for social service functions. The district centers on the junction of Route 153 and Mountain Laurel Road.

moments.title: New Hampshire Farm Museum
moments.text: A connected line of farm buildings stretches from a small roadside barn to the Great Barn at the New Hampshire Farm Museum. Joseph Plumer’s 1782 house survives as one of the linking sections. At the far end, the three-story Great Barn measures 104 feet long and houses agricultural tools, machinery, sleighs and wagons. The museum acquired the farmstead as its permanent home in 1979. It operates a demonstration farm, with walking trails through the wood lots behind the buildings. Live farm animals share the property with the collections, and the Great Barn’s exhibits fill three floors.
moments.notice: Follow the connected buildings from the roadside barn to the three-story Great Barn.

moments.title: Milton
moments.text: Milton’s main village stands beside the Salmon Falls River, a boundary with Maine and part of the town’s industrial geography. Water-powered industries were concentrated here. In 1893, Jonas Spaulding opened a leatherboard mill under the name J. Spaulding and Sons. Two sons, Huntley and Rolland, later served as New Hampshire governors. The business opened a second Milton leatherboard mill in 1913 and acquired a company making lunch boxes and violin cases from leatherboard and vulcanized fiber. The concentration of water-powered businesses also prompted Ira W. Jones to establish an engineering firm with offices on Main Street.
